title: GRINDLINE: building a CoD-style browser shooter with Claude Code, Tripo, an LLM "balance designer" and Replay Vision
author: Appropriate_Sail3890
selftext:
I'm making GRINDLINE, a CoD-style FPS that runs in the browser. Claude Code writes most of the code, and the guns and props come from Tripo. A few things I learned:

Give the agent something to measure. Asking "does this look right" goes nowhere. Hand placement on new guns is measured against the gun's mesh, and new sounds get matched to the loudness of the old ones. Today a new rifle went from raw model to playable in a few hours.

An LLM can tune balance if it knows what each gun is for. I had a judgment API (Jev) tweak stats against a duel sim. Judged on average win rate, it kept trying to fix the shotgun for losing at 75 m. Once every gun had a role, it got the guns from 96 points outside their roles down to 6. You still have to playtest it.

Script the asset pipeline once. Every gun goes through the same steps: label parts, scale, rig, add sights. After the first one it's mostly mechanical.

Taste is still my job. I keep a notes file the agent reads every session ("no brass sounds", "less reverb") so it stops re-suggesting things I've already rejected.

For this I also built a framework, Squire changes the deal you make with an AI agent when you build a game. Most AI game tools are separate from the game: you prompt something, get a file, and drag it in by hand. Squire puts the agent inside the running game. Worlds are code the agent can edit, its edits load into the world you're playing without a restart, and every change is one undoable step that keeps your manual edits. The agent can ask where you're standing, screenshot what you see, and check that the code compiles before it calls anything done. It works against a set of budgets for triangles, lights, draw calls and memory, so it can't quietly bury your frame rate under detail. Whole districts of Grindline got built that way: the agent added streets, shops, stairs and props while I walked around in them.

The other half is that everything around the engine is built for agents too. Models come from Tripo jobs and get fitted into the world by scripts. Textures can be generated and applied to one surface or a whole family of materials, and that's undoable too. A gun goes from a generated model to fully playable with measured hand placement, and its sounds get matched by loudness instead of guessed. The workflow above it borrows the same idea: test, measure and watch the game run headless rather than trust the model's opinion. That's why one person can make a networked browser shooter with bots, a Horde mode, a sound pass and launch trailers in two weeks, not years. I'd call that a real shift in who gets to make games this size, even if "monumental" is a word I'd let players use rather than us.

Play it free in your browser: [Link](https://grindline.ryanfitzpatrick.io). Happy to answer questions.
